segments.title: Why refrigerated cargo ships mattered in 1939
segments.body: SS Tairoa was a refrigerated cargo ship of roughly 8,000 gross tons. Ships like her carried meat and other perishables across oceans, an important part of wartime supply during the Battle of the Atlantic. Britain and its partners depended on this traffic, and refrigerated ships were also worth liberating during wartime operations. Tairoa's sinking removed a merchant hull and refrigerated cargo capacity from that long-distance supply network.

evidence.note: SS Tairoa was a refrigerated cargo ship, and ships like her carried meat and other perishables across oceans; wartime operations also sought to liberate such vessels.

segments.summary: Refrigerated ships such as SS Tairoa carried meat and other perishables that wartime supply networks depended on during the Second World War.

segments.title: Tairoa's Brisbane-to-London cargo route
segments.body: This account dates Tairoa's sinking to 3 December, while acknowledging that published dates differ. Admiral Graf Spee caught her during her regular Brisbane-to-London voyage. Her refrigerated holds carried the principal cargo, while "general cargo" meant other goods packed into whatever space remained. The ship combined specialist refrigerated work with a mixed load of additional goods. Her ordinary route was part of the long-distance merchant traffic exposed to German surface raiders in the South Atlantic.

evidence.note: The transcript insists on 3 December as the sinking date despite differing accounts, describes Tairoa's regular Brisbane-to-London route, and explains the flexible meaning of general cargo aboard a refrigerated ship.

segments.summary: Tairoa's regular Brisbane-to-London service shows how a refrigerated ship could carry its principal cargo alongside whatever general cargo fit in the remaining space.

segments.title: Cummings keeps Tairoa's warning on the air
segments.body: The picture discussed during the encounter shows Graf Spee's false turrets and dummy barrels, with a real main gun turned towards Tairoa. Radio officer Cummings began transmitting a raider warning as Admiral Graf Spee attacked. After 37 mm anti-aircraft fire disabled his first position, he found another space, assembled a makeshift radio, and resumed transmitting. German 5.9-inch gunfire finally stopped the signal. The Germans then removed Tairoa's crew, and Graf Spee used more shells and a torpedo to sink the merchant ship. Cummings's persistence gave the British hunting forces a fresh position report.

evidence.note: The transcript points out false turrets and dummy barrels in the picture, with a real main gun aimed towards Tairoa. It recounts Cummings resuming transmission with a makeshift radio after 37 mm fire, the subsequent 5.9-inch fire, and the gunfire and torpedo used to sink Tairoa.

segments.summary: Radio officer Cummings resumes Tairoa's raider warning with a makeshift radio after Admiral Graf Spee's 37 mm fire disables his first transmitting position.

segments.title: What Graf Spee gained from Tairoa's routing papers
segments.body: Some papers were left aboard Tairoa in the rush to send distress signals, and German personnel recovered them. The documents could reveal shipping routes and help identify points where merchant traffic gathered. Their value had a limit: the Royal Navy could read the same geography and guard the likely choke points. Graf Spee could use the captured information, but operating near the locations it revealed carried its own risk.

evidence.note: Captured papers from Tairoa might have revealed shipping routes and concentration points, though the Royal Navy was likely to guard those choke points.

segments.summary: Routing papers left aboard Tairoa could reveal merchant routes and choke points, although those same places were likely to be guarded by the Royal Navy.

segments.title: Tairoa's signal tightens the hunt for Graf Spee
segments.body: Tairoa's distress signal gave the Royal Navy another accurate position for Admiral Graf Spee. The raider was still in the same area as the previous day, so the new report renewed the danger of interception. British ships operating farther south drove north at the greatest practical speed. That movement made the African coast increasingly dangerous for Captain Hans Langsdorff, who had to leave the area. Graf Spee then headed west across the Atlantic, one step in the operational sequence that preceded the Battle of the River Plate.

evidence.note: Tairoa's signal fixed Graf Spee's position while British ships raced north; because the raider remained in the previous day's area, Langsdorff had to leave the African coast.

segments.summary: Tairoa's warning gives British hunting forces a fresh position for Graf Spee, sending ships north and pushing Captain Hans Langsdorff west across the Atlantic.
